[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Technical Tutorial: FastText and Subword Embeddings in NLP"},{"order":2,"type":"subheading","text":"Introduction to FastText"},{"order":3,"type":"paragraph","text":"Traditional word embedding models like Word2Vec (Skip-gram and CBOW) and GloVe treat every distinct word as an atomic unit. While effective, this approach fails when encountering out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words, rare words, or morphologically rich languages. FastText, developed by Facebook's AI Research (FAIR) lab, addresses this limitation by representing words as bags of character n-grams."},{"order":4,"type":"subheading","text":"How Subword Embeddings Work"},{"order":5,"type":"paragraph","text":"In FastText, a word is broken down into character n-grams of specified lengths, bounded by special boundary symbols < and >. For example, consider the word "apple" with an n-gram range of n=3 to n=4. The character n-grams would include:"},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Trigrams: <ap, app, ppl, ple, le>"},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Four-grams: <app, appl, pple, ple>"},{"order":8,"type":"bullet_point","text":"The original word itself: <apple>"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"The vector for the word "apple" is ultimately computed as the sum of the vector representations of all its constituent n-grams and the vector for the whole word itself. This allows the model to share representations across morphologically similar words."},{"order":10,"type":"subheading","text":"Benefits of FastText Over Word2Vec"},{"order":11,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Handling OOV Words: If a test word was never seen during training, its vector can still be constructed by averaging the vectors of its known subwords."},{"order":12,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Morphologically Rich Languages: Languages with heavy inflection (like Finnish, Turkish, or Russian) benefit massively because shared roots and suffixes generate similar embeddings."},{"order":13,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Misspellings and Slang: Typos often share many n-grams with correct words, allowing the model to place them close in the vector space."},{"order":14,"type":"subheading","text":"Training FastText in Python"},{"order":15,"type":"paragraph","text":"The official Python library for FastText (gensim or the native fasttext library) makes it straightforward to train and utilize subword embeddings. Below is an example using the native fasttext library."},{"order":16,"type":"code","text":"import fasttext

# Train a model on a sample text file
model = fasttext.train_unsupervised('train_data.txt', model='skipgram', minn=3, maxn=6)

# Get vector for a known word
vector = model.get_word_vector('apple')
print(vector)

# Get vector for an Out-Of-Vocabulary (OOV) word
oov_vector = model.get_word_vector('applet')
print(oov_vector)"},{"order":17,"type":"subheading","text":"Hyperparameters to Consider"},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"minn and maxn: Define the minimum and maximum lengths of character n-grams. Typical values are minn=3 and maxn=6."},{"order":19,"type":"bullet_point","text":"dim: The dimensionality of the word vectors (commonly 100, 300)."},{"order":20,"type":"bullet_point","text":"ws: The size of the context window."},{"order":21,"type":"subheading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":22,"type":"paragraph","text":"FastText provides a robust upgrade to traditional static embeddings by looking inside the words themselves. By leveraging subword information, NLP pipelines become more resilient to noise, typos, and vocabulary sparsity."}]
